comment: Every engine measured here, with the version it is pinned to.
A benchmark that says an engine is slow without saying which version it
measured is worth nothing, so the pin is written down here, checked into
the repository, and compared against the registry once a week by
cmd/kura-versions. When one of these goes stale the weekly run opens an
issue rather than quietly leaving the numbers describing last year.

engines.name: bleve
engines.note: Its segment library, zapx, is held above the version this release of bleve asks for. The one it asks for cannot read back the postings of a term that appears in more than a thousand documents, so the engine indexes the corpus and then answers nothing.

engines.name: sqlitefts
engines.note: SQLite FTS5 through the pure Go translation, so it runs with cgo off like everything else here.

engines.name: turbovec
engines.note: Ranks by maximum inner product, so it is only ever run against inner product ground truth. Its bit width is fixed when the index is built, so each operating point is a separate index.

engines.name: hnsw
engines.note: Euclidean and cosine. Built at the connection and construction settings hnswlib has defaulted to for years rather than settings picked for this benchmark.

engines.name: exact
engines.note: The brute force scan. It has no library behind it, so there is no version to fall behind, and it is what every approximate index in the vector table is measured against.

engines.name: csr
engines.note: A compressed sparse row adjacency and nothing else. It has no library behind it, so there is no version to fall behind, and it is the layout every other graph store in the table is trying to beat.

engines.name: petgraph
engines.note: The operations are written against its adjacency rather than its algorithm module, because those algorithms make different definitional choices and two engines answering different questions cannot be compared.

engines.name: sqlite
engines.note: Two integer columns and a covering index on both, which is the design a lot of software already has and the floor a graph store has to beat.

engines.name: ladybug
engines.note: The only real graph database in the table. It is linked against the prebuilt shared library its releases publish rather than built from source, which is what makes it possible to measure it on every platform here. Its PageRank is in an extension that downloads at first use, so that row is left empty rather than filled with a number that measured the network.

engines.name: genba
engines.note: Ours. Pinned to a commit rather than a tag until there is a release to pin to. It drops stopwords from a query before running it, which no other engine here does, so its hit counts on a query containing one are lower and its latencies for that query are not comparable.
